- Dispersion strengthening: dispersed CeO2 particles impede dislocation motion (Orowan looping and particle–dislocation interactions), increasing yield stress and microhardness.
- Interlamellar / pore effects: small nanoparticles can fill or interrupt interlamellar voids and reduce open porosity and crack initiation sites, improving cohesive strength and hardness. Reduced porosity also eliminates stress concentrators and increases measured hardness.
- Negative cases: poorly dispersed CeO2 (agglomerates) or a high oxide fraction at splat boundaries can create weak interfaces, gas entrapment, or brittle oxide networks that increase effective porosity or lower load transfer — reducing hardness and toughness.

Relation between porosity and hardness
- Porosity and hardness are inversely related: increasing pore volume reduces cohesive splat bonding and the effective area resisting indentations, so microhardness drops. Thus any CeO2 effect that lowers porosity will contribute to higher hardness; any effect that raises porosity (agglomeration, oxygen-rich interfaces) will reduce hardness despite the presence of hard particles.

Practical caveats
- Outcome depends on CeO2 content, particle size and surface state, powder preparation (dispersion or core–shell), and HVOF parameters (particle heating/deformation, oxidation). Small, well‑distributed amounts improve density and hardness; excessive loading or poor dispersion can be detrimental.
- Hardness increases from CeO2 additions are a composite result of dispersion and porosity effects; reported magnitudes vary with process and measurement method.

Short answer
With increasing annealing time the interfacial (peel/stripping) resistance of cold‑sprayed metallic coatings typically rises at first to a maximum and then falls for longer holds. The early increase is driven by recovery/recrystallization, sintering-like diffusion across splat interfaces and closure of voids/cracks; the later decrease is caused by grain growth/softening, loss of dislocation‑strengthening and by coarsening/oxidation or phase changes that embrittle or weaken interfaces.

Key microstructural mechanisms (time sequence)
- Short times (minutes → short hours, depending on temperature)
  - Recovery and partial recrystallization remove highly strained substructure inside splats and at interfaces, relax residual stresses and allow plastic accommodation across boundaries.
  - Solid‑state diffusion and local atomic rearrangement at splat–splat contacts increase true contact area (necking) and convert mechanical contacts into metallurgical bonds.
  - Pores and microcracks at interfaces shrink or close (sintering effect), improving load transfer and shifting failure from interfacial decohesion to cohesive fracture inside particles.
  → Net effect: increased interfacial cohesion and higher stripping resistance.

- Intermediate times (optimum hold)
  - Recrystallization is largely complete and interparticle metallurgical bonding is maximized. A balance of adequate strength and toughness typically gives the maximum stripping resistance.

- Long times (over‑anneal / extended holds)
  - Grain growth reduces grain‑boundary area and overall strength/toughness (softening, loss of work‑hardening).
  - Annihilation of dislocation structures that contributed to hardness and crack‑arresting reduces resistance to crack initiation and propagation.
  - Coarsening of second phases, thickening or reorganization of oxides at interfaces, or formation of brittle intermetallics/precipitates (system dependent) can embrittle interfaces or reintroduce weak planes.
  - Differential thermal expansion and further diffusion can generate voids or debonding at interfaces.
  → Net effect: reduced stripping resistance after the peak.

Important caveats and practical points
- The exact time at which the maximum occurs depends strongly on temperature, material chemistry, initial deformation state, and annealing atmosphere. Low‑temperature short anneals may give only recovery; higher temperature/longer times accelerate diffusion, grain growth and phase changes.
- Annealing atmosphere matters: inert/reducing ambients favor sintering and bonding without oxide thickening; oxidizing atmospheres can produce interfacial oxide growth that degrades bonding with time.
- Some systems (e.g., those prone to beneficial precipitation or stable oxide removal) may show extended improvement, whereas systems that form embrittling phases will degrade sooner.
- To maximize stripping resistance, choose an anneal schedule that achieves interface healing/metallurgical bonding but avoids over‑annealing (grain growth, over‑softening, or detrimental phase formation).

Direct answer
Mixed hard–soft powder blends enhance bond strength in cold spray because the ductile (soft) phase plastically deforms and creates metallurgical contact and a compliant matrix that entrains and mechanically locks the hard particles, while the hard particles promote local stress/strain localization and geometry for interlocking — together increasing real contact area, jetting/oxide-break-up, and interface mechanical anchoring.

Mechanism (stepwise, technical)
1. Soft-phase plastic flow and jetting — On impact the ductile particles undergo extensive, high‑strain‑rate plastic deformation and adiabatic shear at the interface. That produces particle/substrate jetting and fragments or displaces the native oxide layers, exposing fresh metal and enabling metallurgical contact over larger areas.

2. Envelopment / carrier (scaffolding) effect — Deforming soft particles spread around and partially envelop harder particles and asperities on the substrate, physically embedding the hard particles and binding them into a continuous metallic matrix. The soft matrix therefore carries hard particles to the deposit at lower effective critical velocities than hard particles alone.

3. Localized strain amplification by hard inclusions — Hard particles act as rigid inclusions that concentrate stress and strain gradients in the surrounding soft matrix during impact. These localizations promote adiabatic shear, plastic flow, and oxide rupture adjacent to the inclusions, increasing localized bonding.

4. Mechanical interlocking and geometric anchoring — Non‑deforming or partially deforming hard particles form protrusions and interstitial geometry inside the coating and against the substrate roughness. This creates mechanical interlocks that raise resistance to tensile/shear separation.

5. Porosity reduction and load transfer — A ductile continuous phase fills gaps between hard particles, lowering porosity and enabling effective load transfer across the interface, so cohesive and adhesive strengths increase.

Important caveats and limits
- Balance matters: too high fraction or too large hard particles reduce overall deformability and deposition efficiency and can lower bond strength (insufficient oxide-breakup and jetting).  
- Hard particles (especially ceramics) generally do not metallurgically bond; their benefit is mainly mechanical anchoring and strain localization in the soft matrix.  
- Optimal improvements depend on relative hardness, particle size, volume fraction, and spray velocity/temperature; the soft matrix must be deformable at the chosen spray conditions to realize the above mechanisms.

Because porosity in a cold‑sprayed deposit represents discontinuities and limited true contact area, closing those pores during a thermal post‑treatment converts weak, mechanically‑interlocked contacts into continuous, load‑bearing interfaces and enables metallurgical bonding. Mechanisms behind the adhesion improvement are:

- Increased real bonded area: pore closure and intersplat neck growth enlarge the zones of intimate contact with the substrate and between splats, so more of the interface can transmit shear and normal loads instead of concentrating stress on a few asperities.

- Metallurgical bonding by diffusion and sintering: elevated temperature (and time) activates bulk and grain‑boundary diffusion and promotes neck growth/recrystallization at former splat boundaries and at the coating/substrate interface, turning mechanical joints into true metallurgical bonds with higher cohesive strength.

- Removal of stress concentrators and crack initiation sites: pores and interfacial voids concentrate local stresses and facilitate crack nucleation and delamination; their reduction raises the threshold for interfacial crack propagation.

- Residual stress relaxation and microstructure evolution: heat treatment relieves detrimental tensile residual stresses and can produce microstructural recovery/recrystallization that improves local plasticity and bonding conformity at the interface.

- Improved load transfer and toughness: a denser, more continuous microstructure reduces local compliance mismatches, improving stress transfer across the interface and making the joint less prone to brittle delamination.

Key caveats: these benefits require appropriate temperature, time and atmosphere so diffusion/sintering can occur without excessive oxidation, unwanted phase changes, or over‑growth (grain coarsening) that would degrade properties.

Direct answer
- Compute the aerodynamic (or hydrodynamic) loading on each fin from the fluid drag relation, convert that load into the stress state at the fin root/interface (shear and bending/peel components), and compare those computed stresses to the experimentally measured adhesion strengths (use the measured shear strength for shear-dominated loading and the measured tensile/peel strength or interfacial fracture toughness for peel-dominated loading). If the applied stresses (or energy-release-rate) exceed the measured capability (with an appropriate safety factor and fatigue allowance), the fins will not survive service.

Step-by-step procedure (with formulas and definitions)
1. Get flow and geometry inputs
   - fluid density ρ and nominal flow speed U (local freestream or local approach velocity).
   - fin geometry: fin height H (normal to base), base footprint area Ab = b × L (b = base width in flow direction, L = span into page), fin thickness t (if needed), and centroid height x (distance from base to resultant drag; for a uniform pressure over the fin x ≈ H/2).
   - choose appropriate drag coefficient C_D for the fin shape / Reynolds number (or use measured pressure-drop / force data).

2. Compute the aerodynamic/hydrodynamic force on one fin
   - F_D = 0.5 · C_D · ρ · U^2 · A_proj
     where A_proj is the projected area normal to flow (≈ H · L for an upright fin). Alternately, if you have channel pressure loss Δp across the fin array, use F_D = Δp · A_proj.

3. Compute interface shear stress (if loading transfers as simple shear)
   - τ_interface = F_D / Ab
     where Ab is the bonded area of the fin base. Compare τ_interface to the measured interfacial shear strength τ_adh (from shear tests). Require τ_interface ≤ τ_adh / SF (SF = safety factor, typical 2–4 depending on consequence).

4. Compute bending/peel (tensile) stress at the root (if bending/peel is important)
   - Root bending moment: M_root ≈ F_D · x (x ≈ H/2 for a distributed load).
   - For a rectangular fin cross-section (span L, thickness t in the bending direction), section modulus Z = (L · t^2)/6.
   - Peak bending stress at the root: σ_root = M_root / Z = (6 · F_D · x) / (L · t^2).
     Compare σ_root to the measured interfacial tensile/peel strength σ_adh (or to cohesive tensile strength if cohesive failure is expected). Use σ_root ≤ σ_adh / SF.

5. Combine shear and peel (mixed-mode)
   - If both shear and peel are present, evaluate both τ_interface and σ_root and compare to corresponding strengths. For mixed-mode fracture, use a mixed-mode criterion (e.g., quadratic interaction or a fracture toughness-based mixed-mode law) or conservatively take the more critical ratio:
     max(τ_interface/τ_adh, σ_root/σ_adh) ≤ 1/SF.

6. Fatigue / unsteady loading
   - If loads fluctuate (vortex shedding, gusts, acoustic excitation), compute the alternating components Δτ and Δσ and compare to fatigue endurance of the interface. If no fatigue data, apply a larger safety factor or perform fatigue testing. Repeated subcritical cycles can grow interfacial cracks even when static strength is adequate; consider cumulative damage.

7. Fracture-mechanics refinement (optional)
   - If you have interface fracture toughness Gc (or KIc equiv.), convert the applied loading to an energy-release rate G_app for an interfacial crack (or compute stress-intensity factors for the expected crack geometry). If G_app ≥ Gc the interface will propagate a crack. This is the correct method when pre-existing flaws control failure.

Practical notes and caveats
- Use the measured adhesion value appropriate to the failure mode: shear tests for shear-dominated loading; tensile/peel tests or interfacial fracture toughness for peel-dominated loading. ASTM shear tests can be limited by adhesive glue strength—use tests that probe the actual interface strength when possible.
- If you have array-level pressure-drop data from a test rig, that measured Δp often gives a more reliable net loading than idealized C_D estimates.
- Account for temperature, environmental degradation, corrosion, and erosion — these reduce effective adhesion strength and should be included via reduction factors or testing at service conditions.
- Choose a conservative safety factor (commonly 2–4) and include allowances for manufacturing variability, residual stresses, surface preparation quality, and possible defects.
- If possible, validate with a prototype test (flow rig or vibration fatigue) to confirm that the calculated margins predict survival in practice.

Summary checklist
- Compute F_D from drag relation or measured Δp.
- Convert F_D into τ_interface and σ_root (and Δ components if unsteady).
- Compare to measured τ_adh and σ_adh (and/or Gc) using an appropriate safety factor.
- If either stress or G_app exceeds capacity, redesign geometry, improve adhesion, or reduce service loading.

Direct answer:
The Hartman–Schijve (H–S) variant of NASGRO reduces to a Paris‐like law for cracks that nucleate from small material discontinuities when (1) crack opening/closure is negligible so the effective range ≈ ΔK, (2) the effective threshold term is small, and (3) the fracture‑proximity correction is negligible (Kmax ≪ the material’s cyclic fracture parameter). Under those assumptions the H–S expression algebraically collapses to da/dN ∝ (ΔK − ΔKthr)^β, and with ΔKthr ≈ 0 and β ≈ 2 it becomes the familiar Paris form da/dN = C (ΔK)^m.

More detail (compact):
The H–S (Hartman–Schijve) form commonly used in NASGRO is written as
da/dN = D [ (ΔK_eff − ΔK_eff,thr) / sqrt(1 − Kmax/A) ]^β,
with ΔK_eff = Kmax − Kop = ΔK − ΔKop, ΔKop an opening/closure term, A an apparent cyclic fracture toughness parameter, and β (often ≈2) a material exponent.

For small cracks nucleated from microscopic discontinuities:
- ΔKop → 0 (ΔK_eff → ΔK) because the crack‑opening contribution grows exponentially with crack length and is vanishingly small for very short cracks.
- If ΔK_eff,thr is small relative to ΔK (or is absorbed into fitting constants) then (ΔK_eff − ΔK_eff,thr) ≈ (ΔK − ΔKthr).
- If Kmax ≪ A then sqrt(1 − Kmax/A) ≈ 1 and the fracture‑proximity denominator can be ignored.

Combining these approximations:
da/dN ≈ D (ΔK − ΔKthr)^β.
With ΔKthr ≈ 0 and β ≈ 2 this becomes da/dN ≈ C (ΔK)^m, i.e. a Paris‑type law (C ≡ D, m ≡ β).

Key caveats:
- These simplifications apply only while the crack is sufficiently small that closure is negligible and Kmax is far from the cyclic fracture limit. As the crack grows ΔKop increases (closure appears) and Kmax/A effects accelerate growth, so the full H–S/NASGRO form must be used for later stages.
- The Paris form obtained is empirical and local: exponent and coefficient must be determined from appropriate small‑crack data; long‑crack data or closure‑dominated behavior can give non‑conservative results if used improperly.

Short answer
Use the Scherrer equation D = K λ / (β cos θ) to convert the XRD peak width (corrected for instrument broadening) into an average coherent crystallite size (D). Apply instrument correction and consistent peak-shape treatment, and be aware that the Scherrer result is a coherence-domain size (not particle size) and cannot separate size broadening from microstrain.

Procedure and equations
1) Measure peaks:
- Collect XRD with the same optics used for an instrument standard (stress-free, large-grain reference).
- Fit each diffraction peak (or use integral breadth) and determine the full width at half maximum (FWHM) βmeas in radians.

2) Correct for instrument broadening:
- For Gaussian-like peaks: βsample = sqrt(βmeas^2 − βinst^2)
- (For Lorentzian-like peaks: βsample = βmeas − βinst)
Use the same definition of β for measured and instrument profiles (FWHM or integral breadth).

3) Apply the Scherrer equation:
D = K λ / (βsample cos θ)
where
- D is the mean crystallite (coherent diffraction domain) size,
- K is the shape (Scherrer) factor (~0.8–1.0; common practice ≈0.9),
- λ is the X-ray wavelength,
- βsample is the breadth (radians) after instrument correction,
- θ is the Bragg angle of the peak.

Practical points and caveats (especially for cold-spray powders)
- Scherrer assumes broadening is solely from small crystallite size. Cold-sprayed materials and deformed powders commonly have microstrain and dislocation-induced broadening; use Williamson–Hall or other line-profile methods to separate strain and size contributions:
  βcosθ = (Kλ/D) + 4ε sinθ (Williamson–Hall, linear fit of βcosθ vs. sinθ).
- Scherrer gives a coherence length (crystallite/sub-grain size), not the physical particle size.
- Upper detectable limit: line-broadening methods lose sensitivity above ~100–200 nm; if grains are larger, peaks may be too sharp to measure size reliably.
- Use several non-equivalent peaks and average results to reduce effects of anisotropic broadening and texture; rotate sample where possible.
- Choose and report K, peak-shape model (Gaussian/Lorentzian/mixed), and how instrument broadening was determined.

Following these steps yields a quantitative estimate of crystallite size from XRD peak broadening, with the above limitations kept in mind.

Direct answer
- According to the Nix–Gao strain‑gradient plasticity model the measured nanoindentation hardness H increases as indentation depth h decreases and follows
  H(h) = H0 · sqrt(1 + h*/h)
  or equivalently
  H(h)^2 = H0^2 (1 + h*/h).
  Thus hardness rises above the depth‑independent (macroscopic) hardness H0 at small depths and asymptotically approaches H0 as h → ∞.

Key parameters and their meanings
- H(h): measured indentation hardness at contact depth h.
- H0: asymptotic (depth‑independent or “bulk”) hardness when geometrically necessary dislocation (GND) effects are negligible.
- h: characteristic indentation contact depth (or a length proportional to contact radius).
- h*: characteristic length scale for the indentation size effect (ISE). h* quantifies the importance of strain‑gradient (GND) hardening; larger h* → stronger ISE (hardness stays high to larger depths).
- h* is determined by material parameters (shear modulus μ, Burgers vector b, Taylor factor and geometrical constants arising from indenter geometry and dislocation model) and H0; physically it reflects the extra dislocation density required by the strain gradient beneath the indenter.

How it is used in practice
- Rearranged form H^2 = H0^2 + (H0^2 h*)·(1/h) gives a straight line when H^2 is plotted versus 1/h. Fitting that line yields H0 (intercept) and h* (from slope/H0^2).
- The model applies where GNDs control ISE (small depths, homogeneous crystalline response, negligible porosity, pile‑up/sink‑in corrected, and for self‑similar indenters like Berkovich/Vickers).

Caveats/limits
- The model assumes continuum strain‑gradient plasticity and homogeneous microstructure. It can fail when other length‑scale effects dominate (surface roughness, tip blunting, pile‑up, substrate influence, porosity, particle boundaries or decohesion). Ensure the tested depth range samples the GND‑dominated regime for a valid fit.

Short answer:
Spark-plasma sintering (SPS) converts an as‑sprayed cold‑spray microstructure into a near‑bulk microstructure by a sequence of contact heating, pressure‑driven closure, electrically‑assisted mass transport and metallurgical bonding, followed by recovery/recrystallization and homogenization. These successive physical and kinetic steps remove porosity and weak interfaces, heal impact damage and produce continuous metallic necks and grain structures that restore ductility, strength and conductivity toward bulk values.

Multi‑step mechanism (concise):

1) Contact activation and localized Joule heating
- Pulsed DC through the compact concentrates Joule heating at particle–particle and particle–substrate asperity contacts. Local temperatures at contacts rise rapidly, softening material and increasing atomic mobility at interfaces.

2) Mechanical consolidation under applied pressure
- Uniaxial pressure compresses the deposit, plastically deforming asperities, closing macro‑ and micro‑pores, and increasing true contact area so conduction and mass transport accelerate.

3) Electrical/thermal disruption of surface films and enhancement of metal‑metal contact
- Localized heating (and possible micro‑discharges) breaks, thins or sputters adsorbed/oxide surface layers at contact points, exposing fresh metal and enabling direct metallic contact or reactive interdiffusion across interfaces.

4) Rapid, electrically assisted mass transport and neck formation
- With elevated local mobility, material transport mechanisms (plastic flow, diffusion along surfaces/grain boundaries, lattice diffusion accelerated by temperature and electric field/electromigration) grow necks between particles. This produces metallurgical bonds rather than mere mechanical interlocking.

5) Densification and pore elimination
- Continued plastic flow, viscous/creeplike deformation at hot contacts and diffusional mass transport close remaining pores and segregate voids to grain boundaries or out of the compact, increasing bulk density.

6) Recovery, recrystallization and selective grain growth
- The combined thermal and mechanical history reduces the high dislocation density produced by cold spray: recovery/recrystallization produces new strain‑free grains; brief exposures and rapid heating/cooling limit excessive grain growth, enabling a refined, more equiaxed microstructure with much lower defect content.

7) Chemical homogenization and phase adjustments
- SPS promotes local homogenization (removal of compositional gradients at interfaces), possible restoration or transformation of phases (e.g., re‑formation of carbides/oxides or dissolution of metastable phases), and redistribution of second‑phase particles—changes that influence toughness, strength and conductivity.

8) Residual stress relaxation and interface strengthening
- Thermal cycles and plastic flow relieve impact residual stresses and convert weak interparticle contacts into continuous metallic matrix and sound interfaces with improved load transfer.

Why these steps produce bulk‑like properties
- Elimination of porosity and weak oxide barriers, creation of continuous metallic bonds, reduced dislocation traps, and a recrystallized, connected grain network restore load‑bearing cross section and permit ductile deformation and better electrical/thermal transport—bringing strength, ductility and conductivity toward bulk values.

Key caveats and controls
- Effectiveness depends on initial coating porosity, oxide chemistry/thickness, presence of brittle phases, and achievable pressure/current/temperature/time. Some stable oxide films or sensitive alloying elements may limit bonding or require higher energy or pre‑treatments. Rapid SPS cycles can minimize undesirable grain growth, but improper parameters can cause excessive coarsening, phase changes, or interdiffusion with substrate.

Direct answer:
Yield stress in cold‑sprayed metal deposits is the sum of a lattice friction term plus a Hall–Petch grain‑boundary contribution (scales with d‑1/2) and a Taylor dislocation hardening term (scales with ρ1/2):

σy = σ0 + kHP · d^(−1/2) + α M G b · ρ^(1/2)

Where
- σ0 = lattice friction (intrinsic base strength),
- kHP = Hall–Petch slope (grain‑boundary strengthening coefficient),
- d = characteristic grain diameter,
- α = a constant (typically ~0.2–0.5),
- M = Taylor factor (~2.5–3.5 depending on crystal structure and texture),
- G = shear modulus,
- b = Burgers vector,
- ρ = dislocation density.

Key implications for cold‑sprayed deposits
- Grain size effect (Hall–Petch): reducing average grain size (especially creating very fine grains at particle interfaces) raises σy proportional to d^(−1/2). Because cold spray often produces a bimodal microstructure (ultrafine interfacial grains + coarser particle cores), a single average d is an approximation; more accurate predictions weight the two populations by volume fraction or treat them as composite regions.
- Dislocation effect (Taylor hardening): high dislocation densities produced by the impact/peening increase σy roughly with the square root of ρ. Large increases in ρ produce significant hardening but are subject to recovery/recrystallization which can reduce ρ over time or with post‑heat treatment.
- Interaction and caveats: the two contributions are treated as additive in this framework but are not strictly independent — high ρ can lead to subgrain formation and dynamic recrystallization that change d, and very small grains (nanocrystalline regime) may deviate from Hall–Petch (softening or alternative mechanisms). Measurement uncertainty in d and ρ and microstructural heterogeneity make direct quantitative prediction approximate.

Bottom line: grain refinement increases yield as d^(−1/2), and work hardening (dislocations) increases yield as ρ^(1/2); both contribute additively in the combined Hall–Petch + Taylor description, with microstructural heterogeneity and recovery processes governing the practical balance in cold‑sprayed deposits.

Cold-sprayed coatings can be made much thicker than typical thermal-spray coatings primarily because the two processes produce very different residual-stress histories.

Short answer
- Thermal spray: molten/semimolten particles solidify and cool, producing tensile residual stresses (solidification “quench” strains plus thermal mismatch on cooling) that accumulate with thickness and eventually cause interfacial failure (spallation), so maximum practical thickness is limited.  
- Cold spray: particles consolidate in the solid state by high‑velocity impact, producing little thermal contraction and instead producing compressive, peening-type stresses that do not drive delamination. Low thermal strains plus impact-induced compression allow much thicker, coherent builds.

Technical explanation
- Two stress sources in coatings:
  1. Primary (quench) stresses — from solidification and rapid thermal contraction of molten splats that are constrained by the substrate and neighboring material. These are typically tensile in the deposit and concentrate at the interface. Magnitude scales with ΔT and the material’s stiffness and CTE (roughly ∝ E·α·ΔT for constrained cooling).
  2. Secondary (thermal mismatch) stresses — from differential contraction of coating and substrate as the whole assembly cools from deposition temperature to ambient; these scale with the CTE mismatch, temperature change, modulus and coating thickness.
- In thermal spray both contributions are large: the particles are heated/melted so quench contraction is significant, and the deposit and substrate cool from high temperatures so thermal-mismatch stresses accumulate through the thickness. Tensile stresses encourage cracking and interface decohesion; beyond a critical thickness the tensile stress energy drives delamination or excessive cracking, limiting thickness.
- In cold spray the feedstock remains solid or only mildly heated, so quench contraction is negligible and the effective deposition temperature is low. Particle impact produces severe plastic deformation, metal flow and mechanical interlocking; this impingement acts like in-situ peening and produces compressive stresses through the coating and at the interface. Because there is very little thermal contraction and the dominant residual stress is compressive (or small), there is no progressive buildup of tensile driving force for spallation as thickness grows. Consequently ultra‑thick, dense coatings are achievable without the delamination problems of thermal spray.
- Additional practical points: cold spray also minimizes oxidation and porosity (improving cohesive and adhesive strength), so thick layers remain mechanically robust. However, final stress state still depends on material pairs, substrate preparation and process heat input; large temperature rises or strong CTE mismatch can introduce non-negligible thermal stresses even in cold spray, so thickness limits are not infinite and must be managed.

Bottom line: the absence of solidification shrinkage and the presence of impact-induced compressive stresses in cold spray prevent the accumulation of tensile stresses that limit thermal‑spray thicknesses, enabling much thicker, coherent deposits.

Direct answer:
Cold spray produces microstructural changes (severe plastic deformation, very high dislocation density, grain refinement, strong interparticle bonding, low porosity, residual compressive stress) that raise the coating’s strength and hardness via the Taylor strengthening mechanism. Because Archard’s wear law predicts wear volume inversely proportional to hardness, those microstructural changes reduce wear. Stepwise explanation follows.

Stepwise explanation

1. Impact and microstructure creation
- High-velocity particle impacts in cold spray produce intense localized plastic deformation at particle/substrate interfaces and within particles.
- This generates a very high dislocation density (including geometrically necessary dislocations) and often ultrafine/nanocrystalline grains at impact-affected zones.

2. Strength increase via Taylor strengthening
- Taylor relation (in shear form) states τ = τ0 + α G b √ρ, where τ is flow shear stress, τ0 a baseline stress, α a constant, G shear modulus, b Burgers vector, and ρ dislocation density.
- In polycrystals the corresponding increase in yield strength Δσ scales with √ρ (Δσ ≈ M·α·G·b·√ρ, M = Taylor factor).
- Thus the cold-spray-induced rise in ρ produces a quantifiable increase in yield strength.

3. Conversion of strength to hardness
- Hardness H scales with yield strength (H ≈ C·σy, C ≈ 2.7–3.3 for many metals — the Tabor-type relation); therefore the dislocation-strengthened coating is harder.

4. Reduced wear by Archard’s law
- Archard’s wear law: V = K·F·L / H (V = worn volume, F = normal load, L = sliding distance, K = wear coefficient).
- Because H increases through Taylor strengthening, V decreases approximately inversely with the hardness: higher ρ → higher σy → higher H → lower wear volume.

5. Additional beneficial microstructural effects that lower wear further
- Better metallurgical bonding and lower porosity reduce particle pull-out and delamination, effectively lowering the local wear coefficient K (fewer third-body particles, fewer crack-initiation sites).
- Residual compressive stresses suppress crack initiation/propagation, reducing delamination and brittle fracture modes that would otherwise increase material removal.
- Grain refinement and redistributed hard phases (if present) can both raise obstacle density for plastic flow and modify surface/contact behavior to reduce wear coefficient K (e.g., by promoting stable tribofilms or by increasing resistance to plowing).

6. Net effect (combined)
- Quantitatively, combining relations: Δσ ∝ √ρ, H ∝ σy, and V ∝ 1/H gives V ∝ 1/√ρ (neglecting changes in K). In practice both H increases and K reductions occur, so wear reduction is often larger than predicted by hardness change alone.

Key caveats
- Archard’s law assumes a given wear regime (adhesive/abrasive) and that K is constant; in reality K depends on counterface, environment, contact mechanics, and damage modes. Microcracking, embrittlement, or unstable oxide films can increase K or change the dominant wear mechanism.
- Thermal treatments or long-term recovery can reduce dislocation density (lower √ρ), soften the coating, and increase wear unless other strengthening mechanisms persist.
- Excessive brittleness (e.g., from hard particles or over-ageing) can produce fracture-controlled wear not captured by the simple hardness-based inverse relation.

Summary
Cold spray raises dislocation density and refines microstructure → Taylor strengthening increases yield strength (Δσ ∝ √ρ) → hardness rises → Archard’s law predicts lower wear volume (V ∝ 1/H). Concurrent reductions in porosity, improved bonding, and residual compressive stresses further reduce material removal by lowering the effective wear coefficient and suppressing fracture/delamination.

Short answer
Carrier gas temperature links to coating microhardness through a chain of coupled aerodynamic, thermal and deformation mechanisms. Raising gas temperature changes nozzle flow and particle acceleration, modifies particle temperature and flow stress, and therefore alters impact velocity, the degree and mode of plastic deformation at impact (strain hardening versus thermal softening or dynamic recovery/recrystallization), interparticle/substrate bonding and porosity. The combined effects produce a non‑monotonic dependence of hardness on gas temperature — an optimum exists where increased particle kinetic energy and sufficient but not excessive softening maximize deformation-induced hardening and dense bonding; beyond that point reduced aerodynamic acceleration, excessive softening/recovery or increased porosity/oxidation reduce hardness.

Stepwise physical chain (multi-step phenomena)
1. Gas temperature → gas thermodynamics and nozzle flow
- Increasing Tg raises the speed of sound (a ∝ sqrt(Tg)) and changes the choked/expansion behavior of the nozzle. For a fixed pressure ratio this tends to increase gas exit velocity and the potential gas driving force.
- Simultaneously Tg reduces gas density (ρg ∝ 1/Tg) (and changes viscosity), which lowers aerodynamic drag available to accelerate particles (drag ∝ ½ Cd ρg A vrel^2). The net change in particle acceleration is the result of these opposing tendencies and depends on nozzle geometry, gas type and pressure ratio.

2. Gas temperature → particle temperature and flight heating
- Hotter carrier gas increases particle heating (conduction and convective heat transfer during flight), raising particle temperature prior to impact. Residence time, particle size and emissivity control the magnitude of heating.

3. Particle temperature and velocity → impact conditions (strain rate, stress, and temperature)
- Impact kinetic energy scales with v^2: higher particle velocities increase peak stress and strain rate at impact, enlarging the volume undergoing severe plastic deformation and promoting oxide fracture/removal and intimate metal-to-metal contact.
- Higher particle temperature reduces the flow stress (thermal softening), lowers the critical velocity for bonding, and changes the balance between adiabatic heating at the deformation zone and pre-heating.

4. Impact deformation mode → microstructural evolution
- If impact conditions produce very high strain and strain rates without excessive local temperature rise, particles undergo severe plastic deformation, generating very high dislocation densities and often localized shear instabilities that produce grain refinement (subgrain formation/nanocrystalline zones) and substantial strain hardening — increasing microhardness.
- If particle temperature and/or adiabatic heating are high enough they enable dynamic recovery/recrystallization (or suppress dislocation accumulation), or reduce the resistance to plastic flow so that less work hardening accumulates. That decreases hardness.
- Excessively high pre- or local temperatures can also promote oxide flow/adhesion problems or induce interparticle oxide formation, harming bonding and increasing porosity.

5. Bonding quality and porosity → bulk mechanical response
- Better oxide disruption, higher plastic deformation and mechanical interlocking reduce porosity and create strong metallurgical/mechanical bonds; these increase apparent microhardness of the deposit.
- Conversely, incomplete bonding, rebound, increased porosity or oxide-rich interfaces lower measured hardness and can produce softer local microstructures.

Why an optimum temperature exists
- There are competing, temperature-dependent effects: initially, increasing Tg tends to increase particle kinetic energy and particle temp enough to (a) raise impact severity and (b) lower the critical velocity for deposition, which together improve bonding, densify the deposit and raise hardness (via more plastic deformation and work hardening).
- Beyond an optimal Tg, negative effects grow: reduced aerodynamic drag (lower acceleration efficiency) can limit or even reduce particle velocity; thermal softening and dynamic recovery/recrystallization reduce the accumulation of dislocations and work hardening; higher process temperatures can increase oxide-related defects or porosity in some systems. The result is a peak in microhardness at an intermediate Tg where the beneficial increase in deformation-driven hardening and bonding is largest before softening/recovery and/or poorer acceleration/porosity dominate.

Key caveats
- The exact optimum depends on material (thermal sensitivity of flow stress, tendency to recrystallize, oxide behavior), particle size, gas type, nozzle geometry, pressure ratio and stand-off distance. Therefore the Tg that maximizes hardness is process‑ and material‑specific.
- “Higher temperature” can improve deposition efficiency even when hardness falls, so application goals (hardness versus density, deposition rate, oxide control) must guide parameter selection.

Direct answer (stepwise):

1) Pre-impact thermal state
- Laser preheats particles and substrate locally, raising contact-patch temperature and reducing yield strength. This lowers the critical impact velocity for bonding and increases susceptibility to thermal transformations during/after impact.

2) Supersonic impact and severe plastic deformation (milliseconds)
- Particles strike at high velocity: extreme strain rates (10^4–10^6 s^-1) produce large plastic deformation concentrated in the contact/edge regions.
- Mechanisms: adiabatic shear/instability, jetting of surface oxides, particle flattening and folding, generation of very high dislocation densities and vacancy concentrations.
- Microstructural consequence: ultrafine/subgrain formation and severe grain refinement in the deformed surface layers (often nanometer–submicron scale); retention of relatively undeformed powder cores in many cases (core–shell microstructure).

3) Immediate bonding and defect evolution
- Mechanical interlocking + metal flow + oxide removal produce metallurgical contact. High dislocation density and trapped defects are introduced at particle–particle and particle–substrate interfaces.
- These defects store considerable strain energy and increase initial hardness (work hardening / dislocation strengthening).

4) Concurrent/short-time thermal effects from the laser (during and just after impact)
- Localized heating at the contact patches causes:
  - Enhanced diffusion across interfaces (promotes metallurgical bonding and sintering).
  - Dynamic recovery or dynamic recrystallization (DRX) in the most severely deformed zones if temperature and strain rate conditions permit, producing new, strain-free fine grains.
  - Possible partial melting or local remelting for high laser power, producing a resolidified layer with different grain morphology.
  - For susceptible alloys, thermally activated phase transformations (e.g., austenite ↔ martensite in steels, precipitation/dissolution of secondary phases).
- Net effect depends on balance: if deformation dominates → hard, highly strained microstructure; if thermal effects dominate → softening by recovery/recrystallization or new phases depending on cooling.

5) Cooling and solid-state evolution (microseconds → seconds)
- Rapid cooling rates in the small heated volumes can freeze in non-equilibrium microstructures: high dislocation density, fine grains, or transformed phases (martensite) that increase hardness.
- Slower cooling or repeated thermal cycling (multiple passes/layers) allows more extensive recovery, grain growth, coarsening or precipitation, which reduce hardness relative to the as-deformed state.

6) Accumulated layer and through-thickness gradients
- Multiple impacts/thermal cycles create gradients: very refined, heavily deformed and hardened interparticle/interfacial zones; partially preserved powder cores with lower hardness; heat-affected zone near substrate with coarser grains if heat accumulates.
- Porosity, oxide remnants, and cracking can form if thermal stresses and insufficient bonding occur; these defects reduce measured hardness and mechanical performance locally.

7) Resulting microhardness changes (mechanisms and typical directions)
- Immediate post-impact increase in hardness primarily from:
  - Dislocation strengthening: Δσ ≈ α G b √ρ (higher ρ → higher hardness)
  - Grain-boundary strengthening (Hall–Petch): σ_y = σ_0 + k d^(-1/2) (smaller d → higher hardness)
  - Possible transformation hardening (e.g., martensite) or nanoprecipitates if formed.
- Laser heating can either further increase hardness (by creating fine equiaxed grains on rapid solidification or inducing hard phases) or decrease hardness (by recovery/recrystallization, grain growth, dissolution of strengthening precipitates, tempering of martensite).
- Net microhardness is therefore the result of competition between: work hardening + grain refinement + transformation hardening versus thermal softening (recovery/recrystallization, coarsening, tempering) and defect-induced softening (porosity, cracks).

Key caveats
- The balance of the above steps is strongly material-dependent (FCC vs BCC, tendency to martensitic transformation, presence of precipitates) and depends on processing parameters (impact velocity, particle size, laser power, dwell time, number of passes).
- Spatial heterogeneity (core–shell particle structure, interface bands) is common; single-point microhardness values must be interpreted with respect to location (interface vs particle interior vs HAZ).

Start with the given relations for a spherical indenter contact:

A = 2π R h_c
H = F / A

Substitute A into H:

H = F / (2π R h_c)  (1)

This is the basic measured hardness expression: hardness is proportional to the applied load F and inversely proportional to the product of indenter radius R and contact depth h_c.

Remarks about the variables and their coupling
- h_c is not an independent geometric constant: it depends on the applied load, the indenter geometry, and the elastic–plastic response of the material (including stiffness and work hardening). For example, in the elastic Hertzian regime h_c scales as h_c ∝ (F/(E* R^1/2))^{2/3}, while in the fully plastic limit the load–contact relation becomes dominated by plastic flow and the measured H must satisfy (1) self-consistently with the plastic response.
- Because h_c increases with F, the net dependence of H on F is not simply linear. Two limiting scalings illustrate this:
  - Elastic-dominated (Hertzian) scaling: h_c ∝ F^{2/3} R^{-1/3} ⇒ from (1)
    H ∝ F^{1/3} E*^{2/3} R^{-2/3}.
    (Here apparent H increases weakly with load and falls with increasing R.)
  - Fully plastic (area-controlled) view: (1) is the definition; apparent changes in H with F arise from indentation size effects (geometrically necessary dislocations, strain gradient effects) and/or substrate contribution that change h_c(F) relative to the ideal plastic case.

Implications for hardness testing of thin coatings
- Substrate influence: as contact depth h_c approaches a significant fraction of the coating thickness t, the substrate contributes to load support and alters h_c(F). Because H ∝ 1/(R h_c), substrate effects usually cause a systematic change in measured hardness (apparent hardening or softening depending on relative substrate/coating hardness). To minimize substrate influence, keep h_c small compared with coating thickness (common practical guideline: h_c ≤ ~10% of t, noting this is application-dependent).
- Indenter radius selection: R controls the representative strain beneath the indenter. Larger R produces lower representative strain for a given h_c and averages over a larger volume (reducing scatter from microstructural heterogeneity), but increases the contact area for a given h_c and therefore reduces H via (1). Choose R and F together so that h_c stays within the coating-only regime while sampling the desired material volume.
- Indentation size effect (ISE): at small h_c (low loads) the measured hardness often increases because of strain-gradient/GND effects; at larger h_c hardness approaches an asymptotic (bulk) value. Therefore obtain hardness versus depth or load curves (not a single-load point) and identify the plateau or extrapolate to isolate intrinsic coating hardness.
- Surface roughness, porosity and adhesion: these reduce true contact area or cause local failure, biasing h_c and hence H. Use instrumented indentation (to record h_c directly), inspect residual impressions, and filter data affected by defects.
- Calibration and geometry: accurate knowledge of R and correct calculation of h_c (including corrections for sink-in or pile-up) are essential because errors in R or h_c propagate directly into H through (1).

Practical protocol summary
- Use instrumented indentation to measure h_c directly.
- Run multi-load tests and plot H versus h_c (or H versus F) to find a plateau or perform depth-extrapolation.
- Keep h_c small relative to coating thickness (rule-of-thumb ≤10%).
- Choose R and load to balance sampling volume, ISE sensitivity, and substrate avoidance.
- Inspect indents for porosity/debonding and correct for pile-up/sink-in if needed.

In short: H = F/(2π R h_c). Because h_c itself depends on load, indenter radius and material response, measured hardness will vary with load and R; controlling indentation depth relative to film thickness and using multi-load/depth-dependent analysis are essential to obtain reliable coating hardness values.

Direct answer
- Use volume fractions and constituent hardnesses to compute bounding estimates. The common forms are:
  - Upper (Voigt, rule-of-mixtures): H_up = Vp·Hp + Vm·Hm
  - Lower (Reuss-like, inverse rule): H_low = (Vp/Hp + Vm/Hm)^{-1}
  where Vp and Vm are volume fractions of particle and matrix (Vp+Vm=1) and Hp, Hm their hardnesses.
- Convert any weight fractions to volumes using densities before applying the formulas. Use hardness values representative of the deposited phases (e.g., the work‑hardened cold‑sprayed matrix, not annealed bulk).

Why measured hardness often deviates
- Porosity and voids: pores reduce load‑bearing area and lower apparent hardness relative to ideal ROM.
- Incomplete bonding / weak interfaces: poor particle–matrix bonding or interfacial damage prevents full load transfer; particles may debond or pull out during indentation, reducing hardness.
- Agglomeration and inhomogeneity: clustered or unevenly distributed particles make local hardness vary and the bulk mean can differ from the simple volume‑weighted average.
- Particle size and morphology: large particles or non‑spherical shapes change stress fields and effective reinforcement compared with the ROM assumption of ideal load sharing.
- Microstructural changes in the matrix: severe plastic deformation during cold spray (work hardening, grain refinement, residual stresses, dynamic recrystallization) can raise matrix hardness above nominal values — shifting experimental hardness away from naive ROM predictions.
- Particle damage or porosity within particles: cracked or porous reinforcement provide less reinforcement than assumed.
- Indentation scale and sampling: if indent size is similar to particle spacing, measurements will reflect local phase rather than the macroscopic average; substrate influence (for thin coatings) can also bias results.
- Residual stresses and machining/polishing artifacts: tensile or compressive residual stresses change indentation response; polishing can pull out particles and open subsurface voids.
- Simplifying assumptions of ROM: the ROM ignores stress concentrations, percolation effects, load transfer efficiency, and local plasticity — particulate composites typically fall between the two ROM bounds and often require micromechanical models for accurate prediction.

Practical advice
- Use VOLUME fractions (not wt%), use deposited‑state hardnesses, and bracket expectations with H_low and H_up.
- Correct for porosity (reduce effective Vm or apply porosity factors) or use micromechanical/FE models (Halpin–Tsai, composite-sphere, FEM) for more accurate estimates when particle geometry, interfacial strength, or work‑hardening are significant.
- Ensure indentation depth and sampling plan avoid substrate effects and capture representative microstructure.

Plastic deformation during cold spray
- High-velocity particle impact imposes extremely large, highly localized plastic strains at very high strain rates. That creates massive dislocation multiplication and pile-ups (particularly near particle–particle and particle–substrate interfaces), strong strain gradients across a splat, and frequently very fine, highly strained grains or subgrains in the impacted surface layers.
- The increased dislocation density raises the flow stress (Taylor-type hardening: Δσ ∝ G b √ρ), so the as‑sprayed material is much harder and stronger locally than the undeformed particle interior.
- Because deformation is heterogeneous (hard, highly strained interfacial bands next to less-deformed particle cores) and many particle boundaries are imperfectly bonded or porous, plasticity cannot distribute uniformly. Stress concentrates at non‑bonded interfaces, pores and at hard interfacial zones, promoting brittle crack initiation and propagation along these weak paths.
- Net effect: as-sprayed deposits commonly show high hardness and reduced fracture toughness/ductility — they behave relatively “brittle” at the macroscopic scale even though the base metal is ductile.

How post-deposition heat treatment recovers ductility
- Recovery (low–moderate temperatures, short times): thermal activation enables dislocation rearrangement and annihilation (climb and glide), formation and coarsening of dislocation cells/subgrains, and relaxation of internal stresses. This reduces stored energy and flow stress, restoring some ability to plastically deform without catastrophic cracking.
- Static recrystallization (higher temperature or longer time): new strain‑free, equiaxed grains nucleate (often at the highly strained interfacial regions and other high‑energy sites) and grow, replacing the highly dislocated microstructure. Recrystallized grains significantly lower yield strength and greatly increase uniform elongation and toughness.
- Boundary healing and sintering: diffusion and grain‑boundary migration close or shrink pores, improve metallurgical contact across particle boundaries, and eliminate microcrack nuclei, removing preferred brittle crack paths.
- Residual‑stress relaxation: annealing reduces the magnitude of residual stresses (both compressive and tensile components), lowering driving forces for crack initiation and delamination.
- Alloy‑specific precipitation effects: for precipitation‑strengthened alloys, heat treatment can re‑dissolve or redistribute solute and then re‑precipitate strengthening phases. Properly designed solution + aging treatments can recover ductility and then restore a desirable balance of strength and toughness; inappropriate cycles can over‑soften or leave brittle networks, so parameters must be chosen for the alloy and prior deformation state.

Key caveats and trade‑offs
- The extent of recovery vs. softening depends on temperature/time and the alloy: recovery reduces dislocation density with modest strength loss; recrystallization restores ductility but reduces hardness/strength. For age‑hardening alloys, sequence (solutionize, quench, age) matters to regain strength without sacrificing ductility.
- Because cold‑spray deformation is spatially heterogeneous, complete homogenization can require different thermal budgets than bulk processing.
- Optimizing post‑spray heat treatment requires balancing healed bonding, ductility, and retained strength for the intended application.

Short answer: adhesion of low-temperature cold-sprayed amorphous ceramic powders to metals is dominated by a mix of mechanical anchoring and impact-induced interfacial restructuring rather than classical metallurgical welding. Impact events produce interfacial amorphous (or highly disordered) zones, particle fragmentation and compaction into substrate asperities, and limited atomic-level intermixing across those disordered zones; residual or newly-formed oxides/hydroxides at the interface can either assist bonding by filling gaps or act as weak boundary layers. Coating crystallinity and humid ageing change the balance among these mechanisms by altering deformability, continuity, chemical reactivity, and the integrity of the interfacial layer — crystallization generally reduces the capacity for impact-driven intermixing and increases brittleness and residual stress (often weakening adhesion), while humid ageing promotes interfacial oxidation/hydroxylation and pore/water-assisted crack growth that degrade the bond.

Technical detail

Primary adhesion mechanisms for amorphous ceramic powders on metals (low-temperature cold spray)
- Mechanical interlocking / asperity fill:
  - Ceramic particles (or fragments) plastically fracture and/or compact into substrate roughness and create geometric anchoring. On ductile substrates, substrate plastic flow increases true contact area and entrapment of ceramic fragments.
- Impact-induced interfacial disordering/amorphization and atomic intermixing:
  - Localized, very high strain-rate deformation and transient heating at the collision site produce highly disordered or amorphous cascade volumes at the particle–substrate contact. Those disordered regions permit localized atomic-scale intermixing across the interface (even between ceramic and metal) that increases bond strength beyond pure mechanical anchoring.
- Fragmentation and particle packing:
  - Brittle (ceramic) particles often fracture on impact; fragments pack and sinter mechanically to form a dense coating and intimate contact with the substrate.
- Oxide/chemical-bridge contributions:
  - Native oxides or impact-generated oxides can act as a bonding medium: thin, adherent interfacial oxides or mixed oxide layers may bridge ceramic fragments and metal. Thick, continuous oxides, however, form weak interfaces and reduce adhesion.
- Limited metallurgical bonding:
  - Because global melting is absent, classical diffusion/solid-state welding is limited to very near-interface regions where temperature/strain are highest; any true metallurgical bond is highly localized.

How coating crystallinity modifies these mechanisms
- Amorphous coatings (and amorphous interfacial zones)
  - Greater ability to form continuous, conformal contact at the nanoscale because amorphous/disordered regions created during impact act as compliant, intermixing channels.
  - Facilitate atomic-level intermixing across the interface without requiring long-range diffusion; reduce propensity for intergranular decohesion since there are no grain boundaries at the interface.
  - Tend to absorb impact energy by disordering rather than by brittle cleavage, so initial adhesion can be higher when an amorphous interfacial layer forms.
- Crystalline coatings (or crystallized coatings)
  - Crystallinity introduces grain boundaries and preferred cleavage planes; coatings become more brittle and are more likely to develop interfacial cracks under residual or thermal-mismatch stresses.
  - Crystallization during or after spraying can produce volumetric changes and residual stresses that open weak interfaces or delaminate the coating.
  - Crystalline surfaces are less able to form the atomically disordered interfacial “mixing” channels; bonding shifts toward mechanical interlocking and any chemical/oxide-mediated bonds.
- Net effect: preserving an amorphous interfacial region (or maintaining overall amorphous character where feasible) generally favors adhesion mechanisms based on interfacial disorder/intermixing; crystallization tends to make adhesion more dependent on mechanical anchoring and oxide chemistry and often reduces durability.

How humid ageing modifies these mechanisms
- Growth of interfacial oxides/hydroxides:
  - Exposure to humidity promotes oxidation and/or hydroxylation at the metal–ceramic interface and within coating pores. Thickening of oxide/hydroxide layers typically weakens the bond because these hydrated layers are mechanically weaker and reduce direct metal–ceramic contact and atomic intermixing.
- Water-assisted crack initiation/propagation:
  - Adsorbed water in pores and microcracks reduces fracture toughness (stress-corrosion cracking, subcritical crack growth) and aids propagation along interfacial defects or along weak hydrated oxide layers.
- Capillary and swelling effects:
  - Liquid water in fine porosity produces capillary stresses and can transport corrosive species to the interface; if the ceramic (or any binder) is susceptible to hydrolysis, local chemical degradation further degrades cohesion and interfacial integrity.
- Possible alteration of amorphous layers:
  - Humidity can chemically alter amorphous oxide/hydroxide interlayers (hydration, structural rearrangement) and thus change their mechanical/adhesive properties; in many cases this is detrimental.
- Net effect: humid ageing most commonly reduces adhesion and long-term durability of cold-sprayed ceramic coatings on metals unless the interface is passivated, the coating is dense and impermeable, or protective post-treatments are applied.

Key caveats and practical implications
- The relative importance of mechanisms depends strongly on substrate ductility and roughness, powder chemistry and size, impact energy (particle velocity and mass), and initial oxide thickness on substrate and powder.
- A thin, adherent mixed oxide/interfacial amorphous layer can improve initial bonding; thick or hydrated oxide layers are deleterious.
- To maximize durable adhesion: tailor spray parameters to promote sufficient interfacial disorder/intermixing without inducing detrimental crystallization, prepare substrate to allow some plastic accommodation or engineered roughness for mechanical anchoring, and limit moisture ingress (dense coatings, sealants, or passivation) to prevent humid-age degradation.

Short answer
Annealing alters cold‑sprayed Al deposits by a progressive sequence of defect relaxation, interface healing and microstructure re‑organization that converts a high‑strength/brittle, interface‑controlled fracture mode into a more ductile, bulk‑controlled fracture mode. The dominant steps are: recovery → static recrystallization (new grain formation) → inter‑splat/interface healing and porosity reduction → grain growth and precipitation evolution → final mechanical/property changes (reduced hardness/yield, increased ductility/toughness, change in fracture morphology).

Detailed sequence and the mechanisms involved
1. Recovery (low thermal exposure, short time)
- Mobile dislocations rearrange and annihilate; dislocation density and tangled networks fall.
- Low‑angle subgrain boundaries (LAGBs) convert to fewer, more stable configurations.
- Residual (compressive/tensile) stresses relax.
Effect: reduced strain hardening and hardness; increased local plasticity and crack‑blunting ability.

2. Static recrystallization (moderate thermal exposure)
- New, strain‑free equiaxed grains nucleate (often at heavily deformed regions: splat boundaries, particle interiors) and consume the deformed microstructure.
- High‑angle grain boundaries (HAGBs) form, producing a more homogeneous, equiaxed grain structure.
Effect: large drop in dislocation‑density strengthening, stronger recovery of ductility, more uniform local mechanical response.

3. Inter‑splat/interface healing and atomic diffusion
- Atomistic diffusion and boundary migration at elevated temperature weld previously mechanically bonded splat‑splat interfaces: necking, local metallurgical bonding, and elimination of microcracks or weak interfaces.
- Vacancy and diffusional processes partially close small pores and microvoids; sintering‑like neck growth between particles occurs where oxides/contaminants are absent or permeable.
Effect: removal of primary crack initiation sites; fracture mode shifts away from interfacial decohesion.

4. Porosity evolution and defect redistribution
- Small pores shrink or coalesce; some larger pores persist unless full densification treatments are applied.
- Second‑phase particles or oxide films tend to remain as stress concentrators unless dissolved or entrapped by recrystallized grains.
Effect: fewer stress concentrators → higher macroscopic toughness, but remaining defects can still cause mixed‑mode failure.

5. Precipitation, solute redistribution and particle evolution (alloy dependent)
- Solute redistribution can cause precipitate dissolution, re‑precipitation, coarsening or new intermetallic formation depending on alloy chemistry and thermal path.
- Precipitate evolution alters strengthening balance: possible loss of strain‑aging/precipitation strengthening or, if followed by aging, recovery of precipitation hardening.
Effect: strength may decrease (if precipitates coarsen/dissolve) or can be tailored by subsequent heat treatments to regain strength while keeping improved ductility.

6. Grain growth and final microstructure (prolonged/high thermal exposure)
- Recrystallized grains grow; grain size increases reduce Hall‑Petch strengthening.
- Excessive grain growth can lower both hardness and strength but further increase uniform elongation.
Effect: trade‑off between strength and ductility; over‑annealing can degrade mechanical performance.

Net change in fracture behavior
- As‑sprayed: brittle or mixed brittle interfacial fracture dominated by decohesion along non‑bonded splat boundaries and high dislocation density (low ductility).
- After appropriate anneal: fewer interfacial cracks, more continuous metallurgical bonds, lower dislocation density; failure mode shifts to ductile void nucleation and coalescence within the bulk or around second‑phase particles — fracture surfaces show dimples rather than cleavage/interfaces.
- If annealing is incomplete, a mixed mode persists: some interfaces remain crack initiation sites and local brittle regions coexist with ductile matrix.

Key caveats
- The exact temperatures/times, oxide films, second‑phase presence, and alloy chemistry control which steps dominate and the balance of strength vs. ductility.
- Oxide films and large unbonded interfaces can limit healing; full bulk‑like properties often require additional thermomechanical processing (compression, rolling, solution + aging) beyond simple annealing.

Short answer
Indentation measures the coating’s effective elastic response (the unloading stiffness), not the intrinsic lattice elastic modulus. In cold‑sprayed metallic coatings the measured modulus is reduced because inter‑splat interfaces and microcracks introduce additional, load‑dependent compliance and irreversible (or slowly reversible) deformation that reduce the unloading stiffness — a phenomenon described by recovery resistance. The indentation field is multiaxial and activates inter‑splat sliding and opening, so part of the indentation displacement is taken up by interface shear/friction and crack opening rather than by purely elastic strain in the metal. That extra compliance lowers the apparent modulus calculated from the unloading slope.

Mechanisms in more detail
- Recovery resistance concept: recovery resistance is the resistance to elastic recovery during unloading arising from non‑ideal contacts, frictional sliding, and microcracking at interfaces. If some of the displacement under load is dissipative or frictionally arrested (not recovered elastically on unloading), the unloading stiffness is reduced and the deduced elastic modulus is too low.

- Multiaxial stress state under an indenter: indentation produces a complex stress state — strong compressive stresses beneath the indenter and tensile/shear components radially and laterally. These multiaxial components preferentially load horizontally oriented inter‑splat boundaries, opening, shearing, or causing relative motion between splats.

- Inter‑splat sliding and interface compliance: splats behave like stiff elastic plates connected by weaker, frictional/shearable interfaces (and possibly microcracks/pores). Under the multiaxial indentation stresses, those interfaces deform by sliding, stick–slip, or crack opening. That deformation adds a compliance in series with the splat elastic compliance. Total compliance = intrinsic solid compliance + interfacial compliance. Because the indentation modulus (via Oliver–Pharr or similar) is proportional to the measured unloading stiffness, any extra interfacial compliance reduces the apparent modulus.

- Nonlinearity and load dependence: interface sliding/friction is stress‑dependent and can be partially irreversible or rate dependent, so the apparent modulus can change with indentation load and unloading rate. Heat treatments or processes that heal interfaces reduce interfacial compliance and raise the measured modulus, consistent with the recovery‑resistance picture.

Practical implications and caveats
- Indentation therefore reports an effective, structure‑dependent modulus (splat‑assembly stiffness) not the single‑crystal or bulk wrought modulus. 
- The magnitude of the underestimate depends on indentation scale versus splat size/thickness, the density and strength of inter‑splat contacts, porosity, and testing conditions (load, rate, surface prep).
- To access the intrinsic bulk modulus one must reduce interfacial effects (deeper probing into contiguous material, heat treatment, or complementary macroscopic methods) or use models that include interfacial compliance when interpreting indentation data.

Grain coarsening reduces shear strength because it lowers the material’s yield stress via the Hall–Petch effect, and the von Mises criterion then converts that lower yield stress into a proportionally lower shear-yield.

Key relations and reasoning:
- Hall–Petch (tensile/yield strengthening by grain boundaries):
  σy = σ0 + k·d−1/2
  where σy is the yield stress, σ0 is the friction (lattice) stress, k is the Hall–Petch coefficient and d is the average grain diameter. Larger d (coarsening) → smaller k·d−1/2 contribution → lower σy because grain boundaries (obstacles to dislocation motion) decrease in area and density.
- Von Mises relation between tensile yield and pure shear yield:
  τy = σy / √3
  so the critical shear stress τy scales directly with σy.

Combine them:
  τy = (σ0 + k·d−1/2) / √3
Thus as d increases, τy decreases roughly ∝ d−1/2 (the k-term), so grain coarsening directly reduces shear strength.

Additional contributing effects (important caveats):
- High-temperature annealing also reduces dislocation density (recovery/recrystallization), removing Taylor-type hardening (Δσ ∝ √ρ) and further lowering σy.
- At very small grain sizes or high homologous temperatures the Hall–Petch relation can change (breakdown or a reduced k), so the quantitative trend may differ outside the normal grain-size range.

Net effect: coarsening reduces the density of barriers to dislocation motion and reduces dislocation-based hardening, lowering σy and therefore lowering the coating’s shear strength per the von Mises criterion.

Direct answer:
- Reinforcement volume fraction (Vf) increases composite yield strength in the rule-of-mixtures sense: more load-bearing reinforcement raises the composite strength roughly proportionally.  
- Interfacial characteristics determine how much of that reinforcement strength is actually transmitted into the matrix: strong, well-bonded interfaces (and favorable geometry/aspect ratio and distribution) raise the effective contribution of Vf; weak, poorly wetted, or debonding interfaces reduce or negate it and create stress concentrators.

Key relations and mechanisms (concise):

1) Basic rule of mixtures (continuum load sharing, ideal case)
   σc = Vf·σr + (1 − Vf)·σm
   - σc: composite yield strength; σr: reinforcement strength; σm: matrix yield strength.
   - Valid as an upper/lower bound depending on reinforcement type (continuous aligned fibers → closer to exact; particulates/discontinuous → crude estimate).

2) Practical (discontinuous/particulate) form with load-transfer efficiency
   σc ≈ (1 − Vf)σm + η·Vf·σr
   - η (0 ≤ η ≤ 1) is an efficiency factor that embodies interfacial shear strength, particle aspect ratio/length, and stress-transfer length. η → 1 for perfect bonding and long/high-aspect reinforcements; η → 0 for no bonding or pull-out.

3) Shear-lag / interfacial dependence
   - η is controlled by interfacial shear strength τi, reinforcement aspect ratio (l/d), and matrix shear modulus. Short/low-aspect reinforcements or low τi produce incomplete stress transfer (reduced η).
   - Poor interfacial bonding produces early debonding/pull-out and lowers σc; strong interfaces maximize load transfer but can also nucleate brittle failure if excessively stiff and mismatched.

4) Additional interfacial-mediated strengthening mechanisms (not captured by simple ROM)
   - Thermal‑mismatch/dislocation generation: coefficient-of-thermal-expansion mismatch produces geometrically necessary dislocations during processing/temperature change; contribution scales with √(Vf/dp) (dp = particle size) and increases σc.
   - Orowan strengthening (for nanoscale particles) and modulus-mismatch strengthening also originate at/near interfaces and add to σc, often accounted as extra terms (additive or combined via root-sum-square) on top of load-transfer contribution.
   - Poor dispersion/agglomeration effectively reduces Vf (and creates defects), lowering σc relative to the ROM prediction.

Caveats and practical notes:
- The simple rule of mixtures assumes uniform distribution, no porosity, and perfect bonding; for real particulate composites, use modified ROM with η plus additional terms for thermal mismatch, Orowan loops, and grain‑refinement (Hall–Petch) to predict yield strength more realistically.  
- Increasing Vf helps up to processing/dispersion limits: beyond a threshold, agglomeration or interface deterioration can reduce strength despite higher nominal Vf.

Because cold spray deposits are formed by extreme, highly localized plastic deformation of many discrete solid particles rather than by melting/solidification, their microstructure after spraying and after anneal differs in ways that preserve a higher hardness “floor.” The principal reasons are:

- High retained stored energy and ultrafine/subgrain structure. Particle impacts produce very high dislocation densities and ultrafine/subgrain structures in heavily deformed zones. Even after recovery during annealing these SPD-generated features (subgrains, dense dislocation networks) persist to higher temperatures than in bulk material, maintaining hardness.

- Heterogeneous deformation and mechanically constrained domains. Cold-sprayed coatings are a mosaic of heavily deformed rims, less-deformed particle cores and planar inter-particle defects. These internal heterogeneities create mechanically constrained volumes that do not recrystallize or coarsen uniformly, so hard regions remain and raise the measured hardness plateau.

- Interface and defect pinning of boundary motion. Particle–particle interfaces, residual pores, and segregated contaminants/oxides at splat boundaries act as obstacles or pinning points for grain-boundary migration and dislocation annihilation (Zener-type pinning). That slows grain growth and recrystallization during annealing compared with bulk, preserving strength-hardened microstructure.

- Lower process temperature (less dynamic recovery during deposition). Because particles remain solid and relatively cool during deposition, much of the work hardening is retained (less in-process recovery) so there is more stored dislocation structure to survive subsequent anneals.

- Residual compressive stresses and geometrical constraints. Compressive residual stresses and the constrained geometry of many small bonded particles inhibit grain growth and softening relative to unconstrained bulk.

By contrast, bulk metal that is annealed or thermally sprayed material (which experiences melting/rapid solidification and larger-scale thermal exposure) either recrystallizes and grain-grows more readily or already contains lamellar/porous, weak interlamellar features that relax more on heating. Those materials therefore soften more during high-temperature annealing. 

Caveat: indentation hardness averages local microstructure and can over-represent the contribution of hard zones; tensile/yield behavior may be governed by the softest paths even when indentation hardness shows a persistent plateau. The exact plateau level and its stability depend on alloy chemistry, particle size, initial deformation, and anneal temperature/time.

Direct answer
- Using a phenomenological effective‑medium model for a cracked porous solid (Zimmerman‑type), the coated modulus Ec relative to the uncracked bulk Eb is reduced according to
  Ec/Eb = 1 / [1 + A·P/(1−P) + B·C/(1−P)],
  where P is bulk porosity, C is the crack volume per unit volume (crack density), and A,B are geometric/mechanical constants for the host material and defect geometry.
- When inter‑splat damage is modelled as a population of thin, flattened (penny‑shaped) horizontally aligned cracks whose number fraction of inter‑splat boundaries is f and whose flatness is represented by a flattening ratio α, the crack density reduces to C ∝ f·α^3 and the relation simplifies to the commonly used form
  Ec/Eb ≈ 1 / [1 + k · f · α^3],
  with k a numerical constant determined by the crack geometry and elastic contrast (≈1.19 for the penny‑shaped crack derivation used here).
- For small f this gives the linear approximation
  Ec/Eb ≈ 1 − k · f · α^3,
  i.e. the coating stiffness drops approximately linearly with the volume fraction of inter‑splat cracks (scaled by the cube of the flattening ratio). For larger f the reduction is nonlinear and asymptotes toward zero as the cracked volume dominates.

Physical interpretation and key points
- Crack volume effect: increasing f increases the volume fraction of weak/open crack planes, so load transfer across the coating is reduced and Ec falls.
- Shape/orientation sensitivity: flattened, disc‑like cracks (large α) remove more stiffness per unit cracked fraction than thicker/less flattened defects; horizontal alignment is especially detrimental for through‑thickness stiffness.
- Porosity vs cracks: if porosity P is small compared with crack volume the crack term dominates; both reduce Ec but the crack geometry factor makes crack damage often the controlling factor in cold‑sprayed deposits.
- Validity and caveats: the model assumes linear elasticity, non‑interacting defects, a representative homogeneous effective medium, small strains, and that cracks are well approximated as thin penny‑shaped flaws. The numerical coefficient k and the precise α definition depend on the crack geometry model used. Independent measurement of f and α (e.g., SAXS/SANS, 3D microscopy) is required for quantitative prediction. Local indentation measurements can show a larger apparent modulus reduction than macroscopic tests because they sample splat‑scale crack distributions.

Direct answer: High-temperature heat treatment raises the hardness of cold‑sprayed carbon‑reinforced metal coatings via a sequence of microstructure‑and‑interface evolution steps that create new, stable strengthening features and improve load transfer. The dominant steps are (1) diffusion‑driven bonding and porosity reduction, (2) precipitation / carbide formation at defects and the metal–carbon interface, (3) local recrystallization and formation of a heterostructured fine‑grained network, and (4) stabilization / Orowan and load‑transfer strengthening by the carbon phase and precipitates. These steps together typically outweigh any softening from dislocation recovery, producing a net hardness increase.

Mechanistic details (stepwise):

1) Rapid activation of diffusion and interface metallurgy
- Heating activates atomic diffusion at particle–particle and particle–reinforcement interfaces. That promotes necking/atomic contact, reduces unbonded gaps and porosity, and establishes metallurgical bonds that permit effective load transfer across the coating. Fewer pores and stronger interparticle joints raise macroscopic hardness and stiffness.

2) Interfacial reactions and precipitation (including carbides)
- Solute atoms migrate to defects and interfaces where supersaturation relaxes. Nucleation of fine precipitates and/or metal‑carbide phases at dislocations, splat boundaries, and at carbon–metal contact points produces hard, dispersed second‑phase particles. These precipitates (and carbides) (a) impede dislocation motion (precipitation hardening) and (b) chemically anchor carbon reinforcements, improving interfacial shear strength.

3) Recrystallization and formation of refined, heterostructured grains
- Deformed, elongated grains and very high local dislocation densities produced by cold spray partially recrystallize. Recrystallization often produces equiaxed, much finer grains at splat boundaries and interfaces while interiors may remain coarser, yielding a heterostructure with many high‑angle, strengthening grain boundaries. Grain refinement increases hardness via the Hall–Petch effect, particularly where grain growth is inhibited.

4) Pinning and stabilization by carbon reinforcements and precipitates
- Carbon reinforcements and newly formed nanoscale precipitates pin grain boundaries (Zener pinning), limiting grain coarsening during heat treatment and preserving a high boundary area. This stabilizes the fine microstructure and sustains Hall–Petch strengthening after cooling. Nanoreinforcements also produce Orowan looping strengthening when precipitates form around them.

5) Redistribution / evolution of dislocations and residual stresses
- Some recovery and annihilation of dislocations occurs (which would soften), but many dislocations become trapped or pinned by precipitates and interfaces; thus a residual dislocation network remains that contributes to work‑hardening. Simultaneously, relaxation of detrimental tensile residual stresses can improve effective hardness and mechanical integrity.

Net effect on hardness
